prose.title: NullKey vs built-in private folders | Control and portability
prose.description: Compares NullKey with the private folders built into some phones and file managers on unlock, recovery, accounts, backups and where they work.
prose.thesis: NullKey is an Android app that keeps private notes, documents and photos in an encrypted vault on the phone, with its own passphrase and recovery key. Some phones and file managers include a private folder of their own. This page compares the two, and it describes the type of feature in general, not any one phone or app.

honest_case.h: The honest case for built-in private folders
p: A built-in folder may suit a reader who wants to keep a few files out of the gallery and does not want another app. If your phone or file manager includes one, there is no separate app to find, and it may use the phone's own screen lock. Check how it is set up and updated.

It may also suit a reader who wants the phone maker to handle the details, including how the folder is unlocked and whether it connects to an account on the phone. NullKey is a separate app that you set up and manage yourself.

differences.h: One app or a feature tied to the phone
p: A built-in folder belongs to a particular phone or file-manager app. What it offers, and how it behaves, depends on the phone model and the maker's software.
NullKey is one app from Google Play for supported phones running Android 12L or later. Optional biometric and hardware-backed unlock depend on the device.
Many built-in folders use the phone's screen lock or a code of their own, and some tie recovery to the phone maker's account. The exact options vary by phone and app.

NullKey uses a passphrase that you choose and a recovery key that you save yourself, with optional biometric unlock, phone screen-lock unlock and an in-app pattern on supported devices. There is no account reset.

differences.h: Backups, encryption and what you can store
p: Whether a built-in folder can be backed up or moved, and how its contents are protected, varies by phone and app, so read the maker's own description.

NullKey encrypts each item with AES-256-GCM, keeps notes and documents as well as photos, and makes a whole-vault encrypted backup with a read-back check, saved to a destination you choose in Android's document picker.

prose.bottom_line: Choose a built-in private folder if you want a quick separation of a few files if your phone already has one, and read the maker's description of how it protects them. Choose NullKey if you are on Android 12L or later and want a vault with its own passphrase, a recovery key you keep yourself, no account and an encrypted backup you control.

faq.q: Is NullKey the same as the private folder on my phone?
faq.a: No. A built-in private folder belongs to your phone or file manager. NullKey is a separate app from Google Play with its own passphrase, recovery key and encrypted backup.

faq.q: How do I get back into NullKey if I forget my passphrase?
faq.a: Use the recovery key that you saved. There is no account reset, and nobody at Alvento can open the vault for you.
